rules_text:
Rules summary Contents 1 Goal of the game 2 Setup 3 Player turn 4 Game end Goal of the game To leave your opponent without any possible moves. Setup A square game board made up of rows and columns is initially completely filled with stones, alternating between black and white pieces. Black moves first, by taking off one of their stones. They may only remove a stone from the middle of the board (the centre or a piece adjacent to the centre) or from one of the corners. White removes one of their stones that is adjacent orthogonally to the empty square created by Black. There should now be two empty squares next to each other. Player turn From there on, players take turns making a move. To move, one jumps one own stone over an opponent's stone into an empty slot right beyond. Jumps can only be orthogonal, not diagonal . A player may make multiple jumps (thence making multiple captures) with the same stone in a turn, but only if all the jumps are in the same direction (no turns). Making more than one jump (when possible) is optional, but the first jump (and capture) is mandatory. Pieces that are jumped are removed from the board. Game end When one player is unable to jump during their turn, they lose the game and the opponent wins.

[Rating: 4/10] Deceptively simple traditional game that beats for instance Alquerque, Fanorona and Clobber in the "set up a full board then start capturing" category. It is however pretty dry and you probably need to learn a bunch of patterns to play well. May be fine for casual play with a nice board and pieces.

[Rating: 4/10] Use to play this as a kid, they had a set set up at the beach near my house.  Other than being more exotic, it is not better than checkers.

[Rating: 4/10] Weirdly uninteresting at every stage of the game. Beginning is too open and aimless and the end sort of plays itself. Maybe there is a cool middle game in there somewhere if you are experienced, but I don't feel like putting in the time or effort for that.

[Rating: 5/10] Random moves against an AI doesn't make you lose much faster than in those games in which you think hard.  The game appears to lack a sound strategy in the opening and most of the middle game. The endgame, however, can be subtle and challenging. In that regard Konane appears to be similiar to Dots & Boxes. I prefer games where experienced players can tell you whether a move is good or rather bad even in the opening, which might be impossible in Konane. So a large part of a game of Konane seems to be opaque - and will remain so no matter how many games you are going to play.

[Rating: 5/10] Hawaiian game similar to Chinese Checkers but played on a large carved square stone using black and white colored lava rock as game pieces.

[Rating: 5/10] mathematically interesting, but I find it a bit tedious to play.  The early game is pretty directionless and the late game is completely calculable.  Still, it feels very different from superficially similar jumping games, so I appreciate the variety.

[Rating: 5/10] I started playing Konane several days ago and so far I found it interesting. Unlike other games, it forces one think out of the box. Board slowly empties out and number of moves available for both players decrease. It makes you to think not in terms of winning material but in terms of how have the last move.
